title: The First Caliphates
description: An illustrated map of the first caliphates, from Abu Bakr in Medina through the Rashidun conquests, Ali and Karbala, the Umayyads of Damascus and the Dome of the Rock, to the Abbasid revolution, the Round City of Baghdad, the House of Wisdom, Samarra, the Mongol sack of 1258 and the end of the caliphate in 1924.
mapLabel: Illustrated map of the first caliphates, from 632 CE to today
note: Based mainly on Arabic histories written a century or more after the events (Ibn Ishaq, al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari and al-Mas’udi), on Byzantine and Syriac chronicles, coins, inscriptions and excavated sites; each chapter says which it follows. Sunni and Shia traditions tell the early years differently, and the numbers in the sources are uncertain. Spain and Sindh lie beyond the map’s edges, so routes run off the map towards them. Native names are given in Arabic. The map is stylised and not to scale. Lands under Powers are painted loosely.

steps.title: The first caliph
steps.text: When the Prophet Muhammad dies in Medina in June 632, his companions choose his friend and father-in-law Abu Bakr to lead the Muslim community as caliph (khalifa, “successor”). Tribes across Arabia break away, and in the Ridda wars (wars of apostasy) his armies bring them back. Some believed Muhammad’s cousin Ali should have led: the root of the Sunni–Shia divide.
steps.today: Today: Medina, Saudi Arabia. The Prophet’s Mosque holds the tombs of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Umar.

steps.title: Yarmouk
steps.text: Under the second caliph, Umar, Arab armies strike north into Roman Syria. In August 636, by the Yarmouk river, an army with Khalid ibn al-Walid among its commanders destroys a large Roman force sent by the emperor Heraclius. Syria is lost to Rome for good; later Arab writers say Heraclius bade it farewell. Al-Qadisiyyah soon opens Iraq.
steps.today: Today: the Yarmouk river forms part of the border between Syria and Jordan.

steps.title: Umar comes to Jerusalem
steps.text: Jerusalem surrenders after a siege. Tradition says its patriarch, Sophronius, would hand it over only to the caliph himself, so Umar comes from Medina, and that he would not pray in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, so that it would not become a mosque. Umar also sets up registers for soldiers’ pay and starts the Islamic calendar from 622.
steps.today: Today: Jerusalem. The Islamic calendar still counts its years from the Hijra, Muhammad’s move from Mecca to Medina in 622.

steps.title: Egypt and Fustat
steps.text: Amr ibn al-As leads a small army into Egypt in 639 CE, and Alexandria surrenders by treaty in 641. Beside the Roman fortress of Babylon he founds Fustat, a garrison city that grows into the heart of later Cairo, with the mosque that still bears his name. The tale that the Arabs burned Alexandria’s library is a later legend.
steps.today: Today: Old Cairo, Egypt. The Mosque of Amr ibn al-As has been rebuilt many times.

steps.title: Uthman’s Quran
steps.text: The third caliph, Uthman, has one standard text of the Quran written out and sent to the main garrison cities, and other copies destroyed; Muslim tradition records this, and most modern scholars accept it. His rule favours his own clan, the Umayyads, and in 656 rebels from Egypt and Iraq kill him in his house in Medina.
steps.today: Today: Medina. Leaves of a Quran in Birmingham, England, have been carbon dated to between 568 and 645.

steps.title: Ali and the first civil war
steps.text: Ali, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law, becomes caliph and rules from Kufa, a garrison city in Iraq. He defeats Aisha, Talha and Zubayr at the Battle of the Camel near Basra, then fights Mu’awiya, governor of Syria, at Siffin in 657. Talks to settle it split Ali’s camp, and in 661 a Kharijite (seceder) kills him in Kufa’s mosque.
steps.today: Today: Kufa, Iraq. Ali’s shrine is at nearby Najaf, a great centre of Shia learning.

steps.title: Mu’awiya’s Damascus
steps.text: Mu’awiya, of the Umayyad clan, is recognised as caliph in 661 and rules from Damascus, where as governor he had built up a loyal Syrian army. He keeps Roman-trained officials and builds a fleet. Before he dies in 680 he has his son Yazid named heir, and the caliphate becomes a dynasty, which many Muslims resented.
steps.today: Today: Damascus, Syria, one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities in the world.

steps.title: Karbala
steps.text: When Yazid succeeds, Husayn, the Prophet’s grandson and Ali’s son, refuses to accept him and sets out from Mecca for Kufa, where supporters had invited him. At Karbala, on 10 October 680, Yazid’s army surrounds his small band, perhaps 70 men, and kills Husayn. Shia Muslims mourn him every year on Ashura, the tenth of Muharram.
steps.today: Today: Karbala, Iraq. Millions of pilgrims visit Husayn’s shrine, above all on Arbaeen, forty days after Ashura.

steps.title: The Dome of the Rock
steps.text: The caliph Abd al-Malik, after a second civil war, builds the Dome of the Rock on Jerusalem’s Temple Mount, finished in about 691 CE: the oldest great Islamic building still standing. Its inscriptions in Arabic proclaim the new faith. He makes Arabic the language of government and strikes new gold coins with words instead of images.
steps.today: Today: the Dome of the Rock stands on the Haram al-Sharif, or Temple Mount, in Jerusalem’s Old City.

steps.title: From the Atlantic to the Indus
steps.text: Under al-Walid I the caliphate reaches its widest. In 711 CE Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses into Spain, and Muhammad ibn al-Qasim invades Sindh in 711 and 712; in the north-east, Bukhara and Samarkand fall. In Damascus al-Walid builds the Great Mosque, on the site of the Christian church of St John.
steps.today: Today: the Umayyad Mosque, Damascus, which keeps a shrine said to hold the head of John the Baptist.

steps.title: Greek fire at Constantinople
steps.text: The Umayyads send a huge army and fleet under Maslama, the caliph’s brother, to besiege Constantinople in 717 CE. The emperor Leo III holds the walls; Greek fire burns the Arab ships; a hard winter, hunger and Bulgar attacks wear down the besiegers. In 718 they withdraw. It is the last great Arab siege of the city.
steps.today: Today: Istanbul. The land walls that held in 717 still run across the city.

steps.title: The black banners
steps.text: Many non-Arab Muslims (mawali) resent Umayyad rule, which favours Arabs. In 747 CE, in Khurasan, Abu Muslim raises black banners for the Abbasids, a family descended from Muhammad’s uncle al-Abbas. Persians and Arab settlers of the east join him, and his armies take Merv and march west through the cities of Iran.

steps.title: Battle of the Zab
steps.text: On the Great Zab river, a tributary of the Tigris, the Abbasid army defeats the last Umayyad caliph, Marwan II, in January 750 CE. Marwan flees to Egypt and is killed. Most of the Umayyad family is hunted down and killed, but a caliph’s grandson, Abd al-Rahman, escapes to Spain and in 756 founds a new Umayyad state at Córdoba.
steps.today: Today: the Great Zab flows from the mountains of Turkey and northern Iraq into the Tigris south of Mosul.

steps.title: The Round City
steps.text: The caliph al-Mansur founds a new capital on the Tigris in 762 CE: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, which everyone calls Baghdad. It is round, with four gates and his palace and mosque at the centre; historians compare it with Ardashir’s round city in Fars. Within decades Baghdad is among the largest cities on earth.
steps.today: Today: Baghdad, Iraq. Nothing of the Round City survives above ground.

steps.title: Harun and the House of Wisdom
steps.text: Under Harun al-Rashid the court is famed for its wealth; Frankish annals record his gift of an elephant to Charlemagne. Paper, learned from China, spreads through Baghdad’s offices and markets. His son al-Ma’mun backs the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma), where Greek, Persian and Indian works are translated, and al-Khwarizmi dedicates his algebra to him.
steps.today: Today: the Thousand and One Nights, put together much later, still set many stories at Harun’s court.

steps.title: Samarra and the Turkish guards
steps.text: In 836 CE al-Mu’tasim moves the capital to Samarra, a new city up the Tigris, to house his army of Turkish slave soldiers (ghilman). There al-Mutawakkil builds the largest mosque of its day, with a spiral minaret. But the guards become kingmakers and kill him in 861, and the caliphs return to Baghdad in 892.
steps.today: Today: Samarra, Iraq; a World Heritage Site. The spiral minaret, the Malwiya, still stands.

steps.title: The Mongols sack Baghdad
steps.text: From 945 CE the Buyids, then from 1055 the Seljuk Turks, hold real power in Baghdad, and the caliphs keep only religious authority. In February 1258 the Mongols under Hulagu take the city, and the last caliph there, al-Musta’sim, is put to death. Estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to many hundreds of thousands, and are disputed.
steps.today: Today: Baghdad. The Mustansiriya, a college built by the caliphs in the 1230s, survived the sack and still stands.

steps.title: The last caliphs
steps.text: In 1261 Egypt’s Mamluk sultans make a surviving Abbasid caliph in Cairo, a figurehead under their protection. When the Ottomans take Cairo in 1517, the last of that line is taken to Istanbul; a later story says he handed the title to the sultan. In March 1924 the Turkish Republic abolishes the caliphate and the last caliph leaves Istanbul.
steps.today: Today: Istanbul, Turkey. The Topkapı Palace keeps relics the Ottomans brought from Cairo and Mecca.

items.name: Abu Bakr
items.text: Abu Bakr was one of the first to follow Muhammad and travelled with him on the Hijra, the move from Mecca to Medina in 622. His daughter Aisha was Muhammad’s wife. As caliph for just two years he reunited Arabia and sent the first armies into Iraq and Syria. He named Umar to follow him.

items.name: Umar
items.text: Under Umar, Arab armies took Syria, Iraq, Egypt and western Iran in ten years. He founded garrison cities such as Kufa, Basra and Fustat to keep soldiers apart from the conquered, and set up pay registers and the calendar. Tradition remembers him as stern and frugal. A Persian slave stabbed him in Medina’s mosque.

items.name: Aisha
items.text: Aisha, daughter of Abu Bakr and wife of Muhammad, is among the most important sources of the sayings and customs of the Prophet (hadith) for Sunni Muslims. In 656 she led an army against Ali at the Battle of the Camel, named after the camel she rode. After her defeat she lived in Medina for over twenty years.

items.name: Ali
items.text: Ali was Muhammad’s cousin, raised in his household, and married his daughter Fatima. Sunni Muslims honour him as the fourth of the rightly guided (Rashidun) caliphs; Shia Muslims see him as the first imam, the Prophet’s rightful heir. Sermons and sayings credited to him were collected in the book Nahj al-Balagha.

items.name: Husayn
items.text: Husayn, son of Ali and Fatima, was a child when his grandfather Muhammad died. His death at Karbala became the central story of Shia Islam, of sacrifice and resistance to injustice, retold every year in mourning processions and passion plays (ta’ziyeh). His shrine at Karbala is one of the holiest places in Shia Islam.

items.name: Abd al-Malik
items.text: Abd al-Malik won a long civil war against a rival caliph in Mecca, Ibn al-Zubayr, and remade the empire as a state with an Arab, Islamic face: Arabic for government records, new coins bearing words from the Quran, and the Dome of the Rock. Four of his sons followed him as caliph.

items.name: Harun al-Rashid
items.text: Harun al-Rashid ruled at the height of Abbasid wealth, waged yearly war on Byzantium and exchanged embassies with Charlemagne. His powerful ministers, the Barmakid family, were patrons of learning until he suddenly destroyed them in 803. The Thousand and One Nights made him a storybook caliph who wanders Baghdad in disguise.

items.name: al-Khwarizmi
items.text: A scholar from Khwarazm, south of the Aral Sea, who worked in al-Ma’mun’s Baghdad. His book on calculating with Hindu numerals carried them west, and his book on restoring and balancing (al-jabr) gave algebra its name. Latin versions of his own name gave us the word algorithm.
